newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ heading for unprecedended 17th qtr of growth.
newsitem.headline: NZ heading for unprecedended 17th qtr of growth.

text.p: Economists on Monday forecast data on Thurday would show the New Zealand economy grew 0.4 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, giving it a seventeenth straight quarter of growth.
The range of forecasts for December quarter GDP production data is 0.3-0.7 percent, for a median of 0.4 percent, according to a survey conducted by MMS Pacific.
That would give an annual average growth rate of 2.3 percent for 1996, unchanged from the September 1996 year.

"The economy is still growing. If we get a positive quarter growth this time, which we probably will, it will the seventeenth consecutive quarter of growth, which is unprecedented," said Bank of New Zealand economist Peter Jolly.
And, if anything, the growth rate will pick up pace, according to almost everyone from Treasury to private sector economists and Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash.

"As a country, we do seem to have achieved the proverbial 'soft landing', in the sense that we project the real economy will bottom out with positive real growth of about two percent," Brash told a parliamentary committee last week.
"From there, we project growth in the real economy of about three percent between the March quarters of 1997 and 1998, and of about four percent between the March quarters of 1998 and 1999."

The rising growth rate in 1997 and 1998 reflects primarily an easing in the stance of fiscal policy and strengthening demand for New Zealand's exports, the bank said in its six monthly projections, published this month.

The Treasury is even more upbeat. Treasury Secretary Murray Horn told the same committee it was confident its more robust forecasts of 2.6 percent growth in the March 1997 year look likely to be fulfilled.
"If you are looking at the current year, 96/7, we are expecting that (economists') consensus, which is about 1.8 percent, lower than ours, to come up," Horn said.
The September quarter GDP outcome at 0.6 percent was higher than the consensus forecast of 0.2 percent, he said.
"On the basis of the September outcome, the December and March quarters have to be pretty much flat for the consensus to come true," he said.
The main reason for the difference between Treasury's and the RBNZ's forecasts is that Treasury sees sustainable growth at around 3.3 percent against the bank's 2.75 percent estimate.
Driving growth in the fourth quarter was export growth, offset by weaker investment and a decline in retail sales.
But economists said the data is somewhat erratic and too historic to move markets.
September quarter data, for example, showed much stronger growth than expected but moved markets not one whit.
"This market is primarily driven by Reserve Bank statements and CPI numbers. Unless it's vastly different from expectations it's probably not going to do a lot," said BNZ's Jolly.
The independent Institute of Economic Research, in its quarterly predictions published last week, increased its forecast for growth in 1998/99 to 4.3 percent from 3.1 percent.
It has delayed the growth peak due to the new coalition government's decision to postpone for a year, until July 1 1998, the implementation of a second round of tax cuts.

Jolly said early evidence of growth in the first quarter of 1997 was patchy, with retail sales strong but questions about its sustainability and some evidence of a downward correction in the housing market. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
